Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished? Here's a quote from a recent video by Sabine Hossenfelder: [...] I wasn’t offered a job because I’m a woman. I'm not guessing that that’s what happened, I know, because they told me. You see, the guy who was head of the institute told me that, since I'm female I should apply for a scholarship that was exclusively for women in the natural sciences. Because then the institute wouldn't have to pay for me. I met Sabine (at the Perimeter Institute). My impression was that she radiated self-confident knowledge and competence. To the extent I am qualified to judge, she came across as a very sensible, good physicist with a well-earned reputation, who has put a lot on the table in her career as a professional physicist, and who would never pull the “gender card” to complain. The situation she describes sounds awfully familiar, probably repeated far too often at universities and research institutes around the world, even today. Women face a multitude of obstacles, starting with the cultural: the “hard” sciences are often presented as male pursuits, whereas women should supposedly be more interested in, I don’t know, arts, crafts, or raising babies. I suspect that this already discourages far too many talented young women. Then there is human biology: the birth of a child can burden any parent, but the burden is obviously disproportionately the mother’s, starting with pregnancy and childbirth itself. Family expectations may pile on top of cultural stereotypes: The young mother may be expected to stay at home with the children, while the father assumes the traditional role of breadwinner. Obstacles like that which Sabine encountered may not even be based on downright gender prejudice. Institutions may simply be worried that hiring a woman is like playing the lottery: The woman may get pregnant, perhaps multiple times, absent from her position for extended periods of time. But yes, old-fashioned, ugly gender prejudice is likely still present at times, not to mention unacceptable behavior like harassment or worse. I recall a discussion I once had with someone, about Sabine: the person I was conversing with questioned her competence, unfavorably comparing her to a much younger (male, of course) physicist who has not yet published anything notable at the time. It was clear to me that I was witnessing an outburst of classic, old-fashioned sexism. And it doesn’t take much to change the statistic. When you look at Nobel laureates, they represent an extreme, one of the trailing ends of the Gaussian curve characterizing the scientific community. All it takes is a small shift of the curve to the left, barely noticeable in its central part, for there to be an order-of-magnitude difference near the trailing ends. In short, even if I boldly assume that we no longer need to worry about gender bias in the Nobel selection process that may have deprived the likes of Lise Meitner, Emmy Noether, Cecilia Payne, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Vera Rubin or Chien-Shiung Wu, just to name a few examples (if the names are unfamiliar, look them up, it’s worth your time), of well-deserved recognition, the cards are still far too often stacked against women by both biology and society. Writing this reminded me of one of my heroes, a person who surely would have deserved a Nobel prize, if only computer scientists qualified for one. I am of course talking about the amazing Grace Hopper, mathematician, computer scientist, and rear admiral of the United States Navy, at the time of her retirement the oldest serving commissioned officer in the armed forces of the United States. One of the things she is known for may not be universally liked but it is still widely in use today, nearly 65 years after its invention: The COBOL programming language.

Is there a measurable amount of energy in a gram of mass? Well, yes… but no. Yes, in the sense that mass and energy are equivalent. That is the true meaning of the famous equation everyone knows, E = m c 2 . It’s not about converting anything into anything. Certainly not about converting mass into energy. It simply is the mathematical form of Einstein’s statement that the inertia(l mass) of a body is equal to its energy-content. (The c 2 part is just a conversion factor between incompatible units.) But no, not in the sense of energy as “the ability to do work”, that is, putting things into motion. We extract useful energy from things when we can convert those things into other things with less energy-content. Take a quantity of combustible fuel and the corresponding quantity of oxygen. By allowing combustion to take place, we produce something that is ever so slightly less in mass (i.e., energy-content). The difference is extracted in the form of heat or pressure, which we can use to put things into motion. Or take something at a higher elevation, say, a large quantity of water. We allow it to flow downward, while spinning a turbine. The end result is that the water is now at a lower elevation, This means less gravitational potential energy. The energy extracted was used to bring the turbine into motion. But now take an inert lump of iron? What do you do with it? What’s the lower energy state you can bring it to? Without adding oxygen, you can’t burn it. If it’s not in a gravitational field, it cannot fall. It will not release energy either through nuclear fusion or nuclear fission. So… it’s a dead lump of iron. No “reasonable amount of energy” that can be extracted by any sensible means. (And no, annihilation with antimatter does not count. Someone would have to produce that antimatter in the first place.) So yes, technically, every gram of mass is equivalent to 89875517873681764 ergs of energy. That’s a lot. Comparable to an atom bomb. But in many (most? almost all?) cases, only a tiny fraction of this energy, exists as “energy” in the sense of the ability to do work, i.e., bring things into motion. Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Yes, electromagnetic waves have both energy and momentum. When an object emits some light in a specific direction, it is pushed backwards ever so slightly. Similarly, when an object absorbs or reflects light, it is pushed by that light. (Experimental spacecraft with solar sails use the momentum of sunlight to accelerate.) As to sound waves, you can even visualize it. A sound wave is a pressure wave. Recall what happens when a very loud sound wave hits, say, a window pane. The glass shatters. It shatters because of the force (change in momentum) as momentum from the incoming sound wave is transferred to the glass. So yes, sound waves also carry momentum. As do waves in general. Since we cannot observe an object crossing an event horizon, does this mean we cannot ever observe an object expanding out of the observable universe? Will it just get more and more redshifted forever? Meaning there is no “un observable” universe? Yes, to the first part of the question. If you were to watch a distant galaxy, you would never see it cross your cosmological event horizon. Its light would simply become more and more redshifted. But no, that does not mean that there is no “un observable” universe. It simply implies that there are parts of the universe that almost certainly exist, but which we cannot ever observe. And that’s why I added the “almost certainly” qualifier. For all I know, just beyond the limits of the observable universe, everything changes, it’s all dancing pink unicorns in whipped cream or something equally silly. If that is the case, we would never know. However, if we assume that by and large, the same rules govern the universe everywhere, including beyond the limits of its observable bits, then pink unicorns are out, and in all likelihood, the universe is still its same old boring self, mostly empty, with galaxies and stars and planets floating around in the void, even far beyond the boundaries of the observable universe. How do string theory and quantum theory explain light not being able to leave a black hole since light has no mass? Do we need relativity theory to explain this? Neither string theory nor the quantum theory are required for an explanation, and the fact that light has no rest mass (although it has energy-momentum, and is therefore subject to gravitation) is also irrelevant. What matters is that “to leave a black hole” you need to go back in time. Once “inside” the event horizon, that horizon is not a place that you can return to, but a past moment in time. For an observer outside the black hole, the event horizon remains forever in the future. For an observer who crosses the horizon, that event horizon becomes part of their past. So in both cases, “return” involves a) coming back from the far future (from the perspective of the outside observer) or b) going back to a past moment in time (from the perspective of the observer who crossed the horizon). In other words: time travel. You don’t need string theory or the quantum theory to explain why you cannot use a flashlight today to light up a scene yesterday. Not without a time machine anyway. If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow? No, it does not, and that is a very important point. The refractive index of transparent materials tends to depend on wavelength. That is to say, light rays of different color will travel at different speeds in that material, and therefore follow different paths. This is why a lens, a prism can split a white ray of light into its constituent colors, creating a rainbow pattern. Gravitational lensing is different, and this has to do fundamentally with the weak equivalence principle. Gravitation is an “equal opportunity” interaction: It does not care about the material properties of the thing that is affected by it. Two rays of light following identical trajectories will be deflected by an identical amount, regardless of their color. This would not be the case, mind you, if the speed of light itself depended on wavelength. And that would be the case if light was a result of an interaction mediated by a particle with mass. But electromagnetism, the interaction behind light, is not mediated by a massive particle. It is mediated by photons, which are massless, so always travel at the vacuum speed of light regardless of their kinetic energy (which in turn determines their frequency, i.e., their color.) So red light and blue light, for instance, despite being substantially different in terms of the energy of the individual photons, will follow the same path in a gravitational field. Having said all that, it is still possible for a gravitational field to produce a rainbow-like effect, but for a different reason. Here is an example of a simulated projection by a gravitational lens with that is not perfectly spherical (i.e., it has a quadrupole mass moment), of light from a point source onto a projection surface: The reason why the colors of the rainbow appear in this image is not because the gravitational lens affected light of different color differently. Rather, it has to do with the constructive/destructive interference of the light wavefront as it arrives at the projection surface; the peaks and valleys of this interference pattern are wavelength-dependent, so we see, e.g., red peaks vs. blue peaks at different locations. Does energy have a gravitational field like matter? E.g., has a charged cell battery higher field compared with an empty one of similar mass? Very much so. In fact, It is energy that is the source of gravitation. Remember the famous (and often colossally misunderstood) equation, E = m c 2 ? Its proper name is mass-energy equivalence relation. To clarify, allow me to quote the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduces this relationship: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” The answer given by the paper is in the affirmative, but the title itself should tell you what you need to know: What we know as a body’s inertia, i.e., its rest mass, is, in fact, its energy-content. The equation E = m c 2 is not about converting anything into anything. It is simply the statement that what we measure as the energy-content of a body, E , can also be measured as its resistance to motion, m , the two measurements being related by the conversion factor c 2 . That conversion factor exists only for cultural reasons, because we humans have chosen incompatible units to measure mass and energy, or ultimately, distance and time. We do so for convenience. But in so-called “natural” units, c = 1 and the mass-energy equivalence relationship is simply E = m . When it comes to gravitation, the source of gravitation is not “matter” (however we define it): It is the energy-content (more precisely, the so-called stress-energy-momentum tensor, but for ordinary matter, that tensor’s only dominant component is the body’s energy-content). This is the mathematics behind the concept of the weak equivalence principle: The gravitational interaction does not care what a body is made of, only its energy-content matters. What form that energy takes is irrelevant. So what happens when you charge a battery? You increase that body’s energy-content. So yes, its inertia changes and by extension, since the gravitational field of a body is sourced by the same inertial mass, its gravitational field changes as well. The change is minuscule. The amount of electrical mass-energy you pump into a battery when charging it is typically a small fraction of a trillionth of the mass of the battery itself, far too small to be measurable. But it’s there. And it should come as no surprise. After all, even for the discharged battery, the bulk of its rest mass is, well, energy! That is to say, almost all the mass of an ordinary object is due to the masses of its constituent baryons (protons and neutrons). Those baryons are made of quarks, but the quarks contribute roughly 1% of their mass. The remaining 99% is the strong force binding energy that holds those quarks together in those protons and neutrons. So next time you lift a heavy object such as a brick, consider: the resistance you feel when you lift it up is almost entirely due to the energy-content of the strong force that ties its subatomic constituents together on microscopic scales, reacting to the Earth’s gravity. What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity? A black hole does not have immense strength or infinite density. Mostly, no infinite gravity either. Take a black hole that has the same mass as the Sun. Put it in place of the Sun. Guess what happens to the Earth? Apart from the lack of sunlight (which would be bad news for us humans) absolutely nothing. The gravity of that black hole is exactly the same, finite gravity as that of the Sun. Density? Sure, a stellar sized black hole is dense. Actual black holes do not form at a mass much less than about three times the mass of the Sun. But even neutron stars are insanely dense, many trillions of times denser than water. But… this may come as a surprise but very, very large black holes are not so dense at all! When we talk about the largest supermassive black holes, they can form at densities less than the density of ordinary water. It’s only when the black hole is relatively small (by that, I mean, three times the mass of the Sun, which would be “only” a million times the mass of the Earth) that such insane densities are encountered as matter collapses into a black hole. And then, the gravity. As I said, at the same distance as the Sun, a one solar mass black hole has the same gravity as the Sun. Far from infinite. So let’s get a little closer. In the case of the Sun, the closest we can get to its center is about 700,000 kilometers, before we collide with the Sun’s surface. At that distance, solar gravity is powerful (about 30 times the gravity of the Earth at sea level) but far from infinite. And you cannot get any closer, because now you would be inside the Sun. But now take that black hole. A black hole with the same mass as the Sun has an effective radius of only about 3 kilometers. Going from 700,000 to 3… as you know, gravitational acceleration is proportional to the inverse square of distance. So now we are up to trillions of times Earth gravity! And that’s just the Newtonian result. Once we take relativity theory into account, there is, after all, one infinity to deal with. At exactly the event horizon, you would literally need an infinitely powerful rocket exerting an infinite force to hover. But that’s because the event horizon has this strange spacetime geometry: “hovering” means the same thing as moving at the vacuum speed of light. Which, as we know, is not possible without an infinitely powerful rocket. But anywhere outside the event horizon, gravity is finite. And it’s strong not because the black hole’s gravity is stronger than the gravity of another object of the same mass, but simply because you can get that much closer to it. As another example, take the Earth. Its radius is roughly 6,370 kilometers or just under 4,000 miles. The radius of a black hole of the same mass? Less than 9 millimeters. Just over one third of an inch. Imagine something with a diameter of two thirds of an inch, not larger than what one of my cats would produce when he is constipated, a pebble really, that weighs as much as the entire planet Earth. Has there been a mistake or intentional deception in the announcement of the discovery of the Higgs particle? No, there is neither a mistake nor any signs of a deception. We’re talking about a discovery that was made over 12 years ago, and has been subjected to plenty of scrutiny since. A plot like this from the CMS experiment tells the story: What it tells us is that there is a slight bump at a specific energy level (approximately 125 GeV) in what appear to be the detections of correlated pairs of photons, and that this bump is consistent with what we would predict if we had a Higgs boson with a rest mass-energy of 125 GeV, decaying into a pair of photons. This is how particle physics experiments are made. Most subatomic particles are not detected directly, because they decay rapidly. However, we know what their decay products are supposed to be, and we can compare that against experiment. Before its discovery, we did not know the mass of the Higgs boson, and while certain mass ranges were excluded, estimates ranged wildly. However, once this bump was detected, things changed. The bump is not particularly significant visually, but it is very significant statistically. Of course just because there’s a bump, we cannot be certain if it is a bump due to the Higgs boson or perhaps something else. So refined experiments look at more specific properties and correlations. For instance, was the detected particle a true scalar (like the Higgs) or perhaps a composite particle that behaves like a so-called pseudoscalar? There were additional experiments that could distinguish between the two. Other hypotheses were also discarded. So now, 12 years later, I don’t think there’s any reason to doubt the validity of this discovery, any more than we might doubt, say, the discovery of the Z boson or the top quark. One question that may not be fully settled yet is whether or not the simplest, minimalist Higgs model is the valid model, or perhaps something more complicated. It would be interesting to see if we could detect a “triple Higgs” interaction, which is a Higgs boson splitting into two Higgs bosons (or equivalently, a Higgs boson emitting or absorbing another Higgs boson).

What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Oh my, this is a hard question to answer... at least in a form suitable for a Quora answer. Let me try to keep it as simple as possible, which means necessarily skipping over some details, but still. You know what vectors are, right? Basically, quantities that have a magnitude and a direction. You may have learned to form inner products of vectors, but that's a misleading notion on its own right. The inner product is formed between a vector and a "covector". One way to think about it, perhaps, is that whereas a vector may be measuring a length and a direction, a covector is measuring the change of something along that length. So whereas vectors are measured using, say, meters or feet, covectors are measured using "inverse" units of length, i.e., meters or feet are now in the denominator. So say, a vector measures a length in a certain direction as 1 meter. Or 100 centimeters. Someone says that they have distributed marbles with a density of 10 marbles per meter. Or 0.1 marbles per centimeter. So now you form an inner product... between a 1-meter vector and the marble density of 10 marbles per meter. Multiply the two, and you get 10 marbles. Change the coordinate system from meters to centimeters: Now you have a 100-cm vector and 0.1 marbles per cm. Multiply the two and... again you get 10 marbles! The inner product between a vector and a covector yields a "scalar", a pure number that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system. This is important. So then, we can actually "define" a covector as the thing that maps a vector into a scalar by applying the inner product. What do you call a thing that maps not one but two vectors into a scalar? Wait, two vectors? Why would we want to do that? Well, how about characterizing how a force works on a surface. The force is a vector. The surface, a small surface element that is, can be characterized by a vector: its "normal" vector indicating its orientation and size. In continuum mechanics, we look at surface elements and the force acting on them. That force can be present due to pressure and stresses in the material. The point is, we need to relate these two vectors together... and the relationship is accomplished by introducing a thing called the "stress tensor", which can basically form an inner product with this pair of vectors. This also happens to be one of the earliest (early 19th century!) applications of tensors in physics. And this then allows us to generalize. If a covector maps a vector into a scalar, a covariant rank-N tensor can map N vectors into a scalar. Conversely, a vector can map a covector into a scalar; so a contravariant rank-N tensor can map N covectors into a scalar. And it is then easy to form "mixed index" tensors that map a collection of, say, N vectors and K covectors into a scalar. That's what tensors do: establish a relationship between vectors and covectors, mapping them into scalar quantities that do not depend on the choice of coordinate system in which the vectors are measured or expressed. Rank-2 tensors can be easily represented using matrices (though technically, it's only the rank-2 mixed index tensors, which map one vector and one covector into a scalar, that should be written as such, rows corresponding to the covariant, columns to the contravariant features of the tensor.) Higher-rank tensors are not that easy to represent as they require either multiple matrices or higher-domensional (cubic, etc.) structures which are not easy to put on paper. One of the wonderful things about tensors, however, is that they allow us to talk about physics without picking a specific coordinate system! If a vector V and a covector U form a scalar, say, V ⋅ U = 1 , that equation remains valid regardless of the coordinate system chosen. This allows us to distinguish physics (the actual things) from mathematics (the representation of those things) very cleanly. Going back to the inner product, we can of course calculate the inner product between two vectors if we have a corresponding rank-2 covariant tensor that we use to map the pair of vectors into a number. The "metric tensor" does this. The number, in this case, may be the length of the small difference between two near-identical vectors. This turns out to be an effective measure of the intrinsic geometry of the plane, of space, of spacetime. Normally, this "metric tensor" is just a generalization of the Pythagorean rule to calculate distances. But things get more complicated in general relativity, where the geometry of spacetime varies from place to place. So say, take a vector. Displace it so that it moves a tiny distance away, following a closed path, arriving back at its point of origin. So now you have a second vector (the direction of the displacement); a third vector (the direction the displaced vector follows when it arrives back at the point of origin); and a fourth vector (the final vector after arrival). The first and the fourth vector would be identical in Euclidean space. They are not in general relativity. The rank-4 tensor that relates these four vectors is the "Riemann curvature tensor", its value changing from point to point reflecting changing curvature. The relationship between this curvature tensor and the presence of matter amounts to the fundamental statement of general relativity, in the form of Einstein's field equations. Well, that's the gist of it. As I said, I glossed over many details. But hopefully at least it's a meaningful glimpse of the role of tensors in physics, relativity theory in particular. Since the Bekenstein Bound and BH event horizons are the most information dense places possible, how probable is it that they are conscious? I think this question was inspired, in part, by a misconception of the meaning, “information”. Allow me to show two character sequences of approximately equal length. First, this: To be, or not to be: that is the question: Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles. And now this: 8RfUd8yHHftN5juY5MPME1SxwcE7lNOAjjo6Q1jlKyK0hdwk 8DU86TeOGcyJZ1Gk2cEMAtRlBK1G0Sy1WU2xFwJ4sBCeQv15 qBV4pJKGcY28npr4GBDXoJQ1aHw09P9xGrJMqjJ3Jj8pXRWO C5jUXwiEWn2cLNFH91Qxnws3 Which of these contain more “information”? It is understandable if you thought it was the first example. The second case is, after all, just some printable ASCII gibberish, no useful content whatsoever. But that does not mean no information! In fact, if you feed both examples to compression algorithms, you will find that the algorithm does a much better job compressing Shakespeare’s lines than the random sequence of letters. In the end, significantly fewer bytes, significantly less information is needed to fully reconstruct the first example compared to the second. But we don’t even need abstract algorithms. Let me show you what I mean: To b, or nt to b: tht s th qstn: Whethr 'ts noblr in th mnd to suffr Th slngs nd arrws of outrgs frtne, Or to tk arms gnst a sea of trbls. Look at this text. I am betting that if you are a native English speaker, you have no trouble reading it even though almost 20% of the letters are missing. You can still unambiguously reconstruct the original. In contrast, if I were to remove but a single letter from the second example containing gibberish, you’d have no way of knowing what that letter was. There is no redundancy. Everything there is important information. We tend to associate information with order. We think there is more information in, say, in a picture on the CRT of an old-fashioned analog television set as opposed to the “snow” we see when the channel is not broadcasting. But in reality, the opposite is true: random noise carries a lot more information than an orderly broadcast. Of course no one said that that information is of any use. Put enough monkeys behind typewriters and the result may even include the four lines of Shakespeare above. But it will also include all other possible combinations of 170-odd letters and symbols, and you’d have no way of knowing what is useful and what is not. So no, a black hole’s event horizon is not conscious. If anything, it’s the opposite. Imagine your brain scrambled in a food processor. The result represents a lot more “information”! But a lot less knowledge. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space? OK, it doesn't exactly work that way. Gravity doesn't slow time, speed time, or change lengths. However, according to the theory of RELATIVITY (never forget the name!) observers in different gravitational fields will measure things differently. So what takes 1 second according to the clock of an observer in a strong gravitational field may take 2 seconds according to the clock of an observer in a weak gravitational field. This of course implies that we have a spatially varying gravitational field, which changes from point to point. Cosmological models are usually homogeneous models: that is, they assume that on average, the gravitational field is the same everywhere, it only changes with time. Over time it becomes weaker in an expanding cosmos, because matter flies apart and becomes less dense. When dark energy is present, stuff flies apart faster. And the rate at which it flies apart decreases more slowly. The Hubble parameter, rather than going down to zero as matter becomes less and less dense, settles down on a nonzero value instead. Expansion continues. As a result of that expansion, there is redshift. Some of it is just plain old velocity-related Doppler, due to things flying apart. But some of it (over cosmological scales, especially) is due to the time-varying gravitational field. On average, matter is less dense today than yesterday, so its overall gravity is weaker today than yesterday, so clocks today appear to tick faster than clocks yesterday. A signal emitted billions of years ago at a certain number of oscillations per second will show fewer oscillations per second as measured by a clock today. Dark energy does not fundamentally change this, but it alters the rate at which cosmological parameters, including the redshift, evolve over time. Isn’t it true that the general theory of relativity suggests the existence of black holes, white holes, negative value e=mc2 energy, wormholes, quantum entanglement, cosmological, constant gravitational waves, and a host of other amazing things? No. General relativity does not “suggest” any of the above. General relativity provides one thing: a set of equations that govern the behavior of the gravitational field. That’s it. End of story. R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G T μ ν . That is all. This equation has many solutions, just like Maxwell’s equations for the electromagnetic field have many solutions. Just because something is a solution of the field equations of a theory does not mean that this solution represents physical reality. Solutions for equations like this one are constrained by conditions. These could be “boundary conditions” (e.g., the expectation that the field vanishes large distances from a source). These could be symmetry conditions (e.g., the expectation that a compact mass has a spherical gravitational field that does not depend on time.) These expectations narrow down the range of solutions. So let’s pick apart the specific points listed in the question. Well, I hope my answer puts those questions into a proper perspective. We can be impressed by the magnificence of Nature and be grateful for our ability in these modern times to actually make sense of some of it without turning explanations into science-fiction fairy tales. Nothing wrong with science-fiction, mind you; my favorite genre. We just need to be careful not to confuse it with reality. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why can't an observer just inside a supermassive black hole's event horizon escape if the gravity isn't strong enough at that point to tear him/her apart? First, allow me to challenge your premise. To “tear him apart”, you don’t just need gravity; you need tidal forces, which is to say, differences in gravity. Tides happen because for instance, different parts of the Earth are different distances away from the Moon, therefore lunar gravity acts on them with different strengths. Take this to the extreme, and in the vicinity of a small black hole or a neutron star, the differences become so large, your head and your big toe will want to follow wildly different orbits… thus you get torn apart. Never mind that, you are right, in the case of a very large supermassive black hole, this does not happen. In that case, tidal forces remain weak near the event horizon. But then, it’s not tidal forces that prevent you from escaping. It’s the sheer strength of gravity, not how it varies from point to point. We can measure the force of gravity, in principle, by calculating how powerful your rocket would need to be in order to simply hover. To escape, you obviously need a rocket even more powerful than that. And guess what… at the horizon, you’d need an infinitely powerful rocket simply to hover. Yet… inside the horizon it’s not even this that prevents you from escaping. What this has to do with is not so much the strength of gravity but the nature of that event horizon. You see, so long as you are outside the horizon, the horizon remains forever in the future. At the “present” of any outside observer, the horizon will not have formed yet, no matter how long they wait. The only way for any observer to make the horizon happen is by crossing it. Otherwise, it remains forever an unattainable future moment in time. But once you cross it, something else happens. Now the horizon is part of your past. I repeat, it’s not a place that you can return to. It does not have a shape. It’s a past moment in time. To return to it, to escape, you no longer need a rocket: you now need a time machine. Which, when you think about it, makes perfect sense even from the outside observers’ perspective. Recall I mentioned that for them, the horizon remains forever in the future. So if you were to escape from the black hole, to an outside observer it would imply that you are coming back from that future. There we go again… time machine. To sum up: at the horizon, you need an infinitely powerful rocket just to hover. Beyond the horizon (which is a future moment in time until/unless you cross it, when it becomes part of your past) you would need a time machine to escape.

If black holes' horizons form infinitely far in the future, then how can they evaporate in finite time? You stumbled upon a key potential contradiction between two things: But first: it is not the horizon that evaporates. Indeed, contrary to popular explanations (including Hawking’s own, from his popular science book) the actual equations tell a different story: Hawking radiation exists because the black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse and therefore, the past and the future boundary conditions are not identical. It is this difference that manifests itself in what distant observers see as outgoing radiation. (As an important aside, it should be mentioned that the characteristic wavelength of Hawking radiation is around 20 times the Schwarzschild radius. That alone should inform us that the horizon is not the source of that radiation.) So what does this mean? Do horizons never form? Maybe. Does a collapsing, evaporating black hole leave behind a “naked singularity”? Maybe. Does something else happen? Who knows, as the final moments of a black hole’s existence take place at the Planck scale, and we know nothing about the Planck scale, especially nothing about how gravity behaves at the Planck scale. The one thing we do know is that Hawking radiation is not predicated on the present-day existence of a horizon. If it were, there would be no Hawking radiation in the first place, since the horizon, even in classical general relativity, remains forever in any outside observer’s future.

How do objects bend or curve spacetime to produce gravity? They don’t. Seriously, they don’t. Don’t believe me? See if you believe this quote: “It is wrong to think that 'geometrization' is something essential. It is only a kind of crutch [Eselsbrücke] for the finding of numerical laws. Whether one links 'geometrical' intuitions with a theory is a ... private matter.” You know who wrote this? A chap who went by the name A. Einstein*. Objects, indeed all material fields with a nonvanishing stress-energy-momentum tensor, serve as sources of the gravitational field. The gravitational field interacts with matter universally and minimally. Universal, in this context, means that the actual material constitution of matter makes no difference; the gravitational field does not care what matter is made of, only its stress-energy-momentum. Minimal, in this context, means that the interaction is confined to a mathematical form that determines inner products and volume elements and nothing else. A field that interacts with matter minimally can be reinterpreted using the language of covariant derivatives as geometry. Usually, this geometry depends on the material properties of matter; e.g., for electromagnetism, this geometric interpretation depends on the charge-to-mass ratio of the matter particle involved. Not so in gravity: Because it is universal, the “gravitational charge-to-mass ratio” is the same for everything, so the geometry is universal. But that means that everything is subject to this geometry, including our senses and our instruments. It is the only geometry that can be observed, so we can elevate this to a principle, or interpretation, and suggest that gravitation determines the geometry of spacetime. Whether or not we should think of gravitation this way is another matter. Gravitation is more than geometry. The gravitational field has a physical existence. It carries energy and momentum in the form of gravitational waves, just as the Maxwell field carries energy and momentum in the form of electromagnetic waves, such as light. Einstein understood this, hence his advice not to take the geometric interpretation as dogma. Matter does not “bend or curve spacetime”. Matter is the source of the gravitational field. This gravitational field affects everything universally, including any attempt to detect the geometry of spacetime. But spacetime is not a physical thing; matter and the gravitational field are physical things. *Einstein to Reichenbach, 8 April 1926, as translated by Lehmkuhl, in Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326, DOI: 10.1016/j.shpsb.2013.08.002 If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If you were sufficiently close to two colliding black holes, would distortions in space caused by the gravity waves be fatal (ignoring all of the other fatal phenomena like the accretion disk and tidal effects)? Well, technically yes, but by that time you are too close already and you’d be killed by those tides even in the absence of a collision and the resulting gravitational waves. [Pedantic note, with apologies: A “gravity wave” is what you see on the surface of the sea when it waves. A “gravitational wave” is a propagating change in the gravitational field away from sources.] The point is, gravitational waves are propagating changes. A single object produces a gravitational field that changes from place to place but it does not change over time in the inertial reference frame in which the object is at rest. But when we have two objects inspiraling towards each other, no such inertial frame exists. The gravitational field changes not just from place to place but also over time. These changes then ripple away towards infinity with ever decreasing amplitude, much like changes in the electromagnetic field do in response to electric charges undergoing accelerating motion. When the gravitational force changes from place to place, it represents a tidal force. Different parts of a body want to head in different directions or different rates. This can rip a body apart. There are tides near any gravitating object, and tides near a black hole can be very strong because we can get very close to a black hole (they are very compact). When the black holes inspiral, these tidal forces change. Those changes propagate. But they do not get stronger with distance, quite the contrary. And in the end, what kills us is not how the tidal forces change over time, but how strong they are in the first place. Get close enough to the black hole and you’ll find out! A little farther away, though… I once calculated that if you were about the same distance from the merger of two ~30 solar mass black holes as the Earth is from the Sun, you could actually hear the result as a loud rising then decaying sound. Yes, there can be sounds in space! Well, not exactly sounds as we know them, not a traveling longitudinal pressure wave in a medium, rather, transversal gravitational waves in the vacuum but in the end how they travel is not relevant; what is relevant is that at that distance, they are powerful enough to interact with our ears. Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance. It is credible, so long as you clearly understand what you are looking at. First of all, it is not a “NASA picture”. It is a picture produced by an international collaboration of radio astronomy observatories. The collaboration is called the “Event Horizon Telescope”, and they spent several years observing M87* to obtain a sufficient amount of data. The picture was synthesized from these observations. These radio telescopes, far apart, formed effectively a single instrument using a technique called very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Basically, the radio telescopes received signals from the same source, and these signals were then phase coherently recombined. The recombined signal was than fitted against various source models, including models of the M87 black hole as well as alternatives. The best-fit model wins! With the help of this model, the radio astronomy data was then processed to form an image. The image depicts “light” (radio waves) generated in the vicinity of and behind the black hole, partially obscured by the black hole’s so-called photon sphere. The result is the famous synthesized image, its color chosen for purely artistic reasons. So it is an image that is a result of credible science. But no, it is not a NASA image. Nor is it an actual photograph: the image was synthesized using a very complex set of methods, processing several years’ worth of observations made by a worldwide collaboration of radio telescopes. And there is certainly plenty of room there for knowledgeable criticism of the observations, their interpretations, the models and the methods. Such criticisms and questions did, in fact, appear since in the scientific literature. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Are ANY particles "real"? Or is every particle a excitation of some QCD field? Are protons therefore, excitations in a quark-gluon field? What about neutrinos? Yes, all elementary particles are excitations of the corresponding quantum fields. (Composite particles, like the proton, are bound states of such excitations.) But ultimately, what is “real” and what is not “real” is a metaphysical question. So let’s start with a practical definition: Something is “real” if two observers agree on it, regardless of their own motion. For instance, absolute motion is not “real”: to an observer moving along with the object, the object will appear motionless. But relative motion is “real”: If one observer sees two objects moving at different speeds and/or in different directions, all other observers will see the same. The actual values will be observer-dependent, but no observer will see these two objects as not moving relative to each other. So in this vein, are particles real? Perhaps not. The particle-content that an observer sees may depend on that observer’s motion. An observer who is accelerating in an otherwise empty universe will see Unruh radiation, photons arriving from the apparent (Rindler) horizon that characterizes his acceleration. An inertial observer will see no Unruh radiation. Actually, the picture gets more complicated, since in order to actually “see” that Unruh radiation, the observer must interact with the electromagnetic field, which ultimately involves charges, so the inertial observer now sees the accelerating observer carrying accelerating charges and thus producing electromagnetic radiation… The devil is in the details, but the end result is that the two observers’ observed particle content is not the same. On a tad more technical level, it boils down to decomposing fields using a Fourier transform. What is the basis for that transform? The decomposition is not unique when accelerating reference frames are permitted. Decompositions with respect to different reference frames correspond to different descriptions of the same field in terms of particle-content. Having said that… as I said, “real” is in the eye of the beholder. When an electron hits the fluorescent screen of an old school CRT causing a flash of light that we see… how can we possibly say that this electron is not “real”? We may know that it is “only” an excitation of the electron field, and that a rapidly accelerating observer nearby might see, e.g., additional electron-positron pairs that we don’t see, but so what? The screen flashed. That’s an event. And ultimately, events are “real”, however they are interpreted in different observer reference frames, with whatever particle content might be associated with the event in these frames.

Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? Brian Greene’s “explanation” is one of many popularizations of physics that are intended to make difficult topics accessible to the “unwashed masses” but in reality, achieve the exact opposite. I would put it in the same basket in which I put the “rubber sheet” analogy of gravity, the “expanding balloon” description of cosmic expansion, even the “miniature solar system” models of the atom. Then I would put that basket out onto the curbside for collection. No, particles do not “burrow through” anything. If they “burrowed” through anything, that would mean a loss of kinetic energy through dissipative processes. Soon enough, everything would come to a halt, floating in some sticky molasses I suppose… But no, I swear, that is not how the Higgs works. Remember that mass is energy? No, mass is not “converted” into energy or vice versa. What we call inertial mass, or rest mass, is the internal energy-content of a thing. That’s what E = m c 2 is about, not about nuclear energy or converting anything into anything: It literally tells you that mass and (internal) energy are the same thing. Equivalent. Unsurprisingly, the equation itself is called the mass-energy equivalence relationship. In the Standard Model of particle physics, most particles start off as massless particles, but they interact with the Higgs field. However, the Higgs field has a very peculiar property. In empty space (i.e., the lowest energy state achievable, the vacuum) the Higgs field itself is not “empty”, so to speak. So particles can interact with it even when there’s supposedly nothing there. In effect, particles interact with the vacuum. Interaction means potential energy. (E.g., when two objects interact by, say, repelling one another, you need to invest energy to push them together, and that energy will be “stored” as their interaction energy while they are close to each other.) When an initially massless electron, for instance, interacts with the vacuum, it means it carries that interaction energy with it, no matter what it does or where it goes. And because the vacuum is everywhere, so to speak, the electron cannot get rid of that interaction energy. It’s always there. That interaction energy shows up, for all practical intents and purposes, as part of the energy-content of that electron. And as I stated above, energy-content means inertial mass. So the electron behaves as a massive particle, because no matter where it goes, what it does, it carries along that interaction energy with the vacuum Higgs field (to be more precise, the so-called vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v., of the Higgs field). So I stress, no “burrowing” is involved. The Higgs field has no rest frame, and how fast or how slow the particle moves with respect to this non-existent rest frame is irrelevant. In its own reference frame, a particle is always at rest. But it still has inertial mass, because the potential energy of its interaction with the Higgs field is there, no matter what.

Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? We detect particles by detecting their interactions with other particles. The strength (or weakness) of the coupling between the particles determines the “cross-section”, basically the likelihood, that a detectable interaction occurs. When the coupling is really, really weak, such interactions occur very rarely. In a 2012 lecture[1], the late Freeman Dyson presented an interesting calculation. The Sun, on account of being hot, emits not only thermal electromagnetic radiation but also thermal gravitational radiation. The same blackbody spectrum, just gravitons, not photons. Sure, gravity is very weak compared to electromagnetism, so instead of the several hundred septillion watts that it emits in the electromagnetic spectrum, the Sun “only” emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation, but that is still a respectable radiating power. If we had a 79 megawatt light bulb at 1 astronomical unit (the Sun-Earth distance) from here, we’d have no trouble detecting it, and no trouble detecting individual photon events from that source using a suitable detector. But this 79 megawatts is not in the form of electromagnetic waves but in the form of gravitational waves. Now Dyson imagined using the entire Earth, every last bit of it, as kind of a “perfect” graviton detector: That is, he assumed that we can somehow monitor the entire Earth in a completely noise-free setting, and detect a single atomic transition (an electron jumping to a higher orbit) as a result of capturing a graviton. I.e., direct detection of a graviton, much the same way we can detect photons with a suitable detector. The result: Dyson’s calculation told us that we would see, on average, one such graviton event every billion years or so. That is what it means to have a very weak coupling between the gravitational field and matter. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Was Heisenberg the first one to promote the use of tensors in physics? No, it was not Heisenberg. Let me show you a snapshot from a page from an interesting paper: Sure, the notation is a bit archaic, but what you are looking at is the Cauchy stress tensor, which characterizes the stresses and pressures in a medium. This snapshot is from a later reprint of Cauchy’s 1827 paper, De la pression ou tension dans un corps solide [Ex. Math. 2 (1827) p. 42]. So as you can see, tensors were already in use in mathematical physics two centuries ago. Later, in the early 20th century, tensors became the essential tool for relativity theory, especially general relativity. The reason is that the tensor concept perfectly captures the difference between the geometric object (which exists independently of any choice of coordinates) vs. its representation in a specific coordinate system. The independence of physics from the coordinates used to represent it is a fundamental concept in relativity theory (and, well, modern physics in general). Heisenberg, incidentally, did not use tensors much to my knowledge. His matrix mechanics was something else: it was a means to represent the observables of quantum physics, for instance, positions and momenta that do not behave like the ordinary numbers of classical physics, specifically they do not commute under multiplication. Later it was shown that Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics was mathematically equivalent to representing the same quantities using function operators acting on Schrödinger’s wavefunction. But those matrices were not used to represent tensor quantities. However, tensors entered the world of quantum physics with a vengeance, starting with the 1930s, with the development of quantum field theory. Does a spinning (Kerr) black hole precess about its axis of rotation; if so, relative to what? No, a Kerr black hole does not precess. It is, by definition, an axisymmetric solution of Einstein’s vacuum field equations and as such, no precession is involved. A Kerr black hole in the process of formation may exhibit precession, e.g., as a part of the famous “ringdown” phase of a black hole merger that has been observed by gravitational wave detectors over the course of the past decade. Precession is not relative to anything: acceleration, including acceleration related to rotation or more complex motion like precession, is absolute. Or you could say that acceleration (including rotation and precession) can be measured as deviations relative to a local inertial (non-accelerating) reference frame, but that is a bit tautological. Why would Americans rather drive their car for days than take the train? I live in Ottawa, Canada. I occasionally visit New York City. By car, a comfortable drive with the occasional rest stops takes about 8 hours and that includes crossing the border. It's 12:30 PM right now. If I were to hop into my car at 1 PM, chances are it'd still be daylight when I get out of my car somewhere in Manhattan. Now suppose I take the train. Google Maps tells me that I could depart tomorrow at 6:07 AM and arrive in Montreal at 8:11 AM. Three hours later, I would depart on Amtrak's Adirondack train, which could deliver me at Penn station a mere 11 hours later, at 10:15 PM. OK, how about return? Well, I could board the same Adirondack train the next day at 8:28 AM, heading back to Montreal. I'd arrive at Montreal's Gare Centrale at 8:16 PM. Too bad, that's after the last train that day left for Ottawa, so I'd have to get a hotel room and board the first train next morning at 6:20 AM. I'd arrive back at Ottawa's main railway station at 8:25 AM, just three minutes short of 24 hours since my departure at Penn Station. This does not include the time it takes to get to or from the railway station but it’s thankfully short, as I live not too far from Ottawa’s main railway station. OK, I could take a plane instead. The flight time from YOW to EWR (Newark) is only 90 minutes. Of course I need to be at the airport at least maybe 2 hours early, to go through customs preclearing. And then there is the ride to/from the airport. So I’d have to leave my home at least 3 hours prior to the scheduled departure, and it’d likely take at least an hour and a half to disembark, get my luggage, get a taxi and get from the airport to Manhattan. Overall? At least 6 hours travel time if everything goes according to plan. Granted, it's a little less than the road trip, but not that much less. And far less convenient. What about environmental costs? Google tells me that with Porter Airlines, one flight option only produces 55 kg of CO2 per passenger. But that's not much less* than the CO2 I'd produce burning up less than one full tank of fuel in my Honda Accord. This gets even more pronounced if I don’t travel alone: That 55 kg is per passenger, whereas my Honda’s fuel consumption would not change noticeably just because, say, my beautiful wife joins me for the trip. Would I like to take the train to NYC? Absolutely. And a century ago, I could have. The Ottawa & New York Railway ceased operations in 1957. I could not find a timetable but I doubt travel times were any worse than traveling with VIA Rail and Amtrak these days. Probably quicker and more comfortable, as a matter of fact. But those days are gone. The railroads may have built North America but today, passenger rail service... well, sucks. *Edited: at first I thought the Honda would produce less than 55 kg, but it’s more likely 90-odd kg. Which, incidentally, is just a tad more than the per-passenger CO2 listed by Google for most flights.

Considering that the event horizon around Sagittarius A black hole reaches millions of degrees in temperature, how far away from the black hole itself would you have to be for the temperature to be a comfortable 70°F? The Hawking-temperature associated with the Sgr A* event horizon region is not millions of degrees. It’s not even single-digit degrees. It’s a small fraction of a trillionth of a degree kelvin above absolute zero. The accretion disk (rapidly swirling, infalling material) around Sgr A* can reach millions of degrees due to internal friction and collisions. At no distance from it would you enjoy “a comfortable 70 F”, though. The bulk thermal radiation coming from this accretion disk is in the form of hard X-rays. We can calculate how far you’d have to be from it to receive a flux that would be consistent with being in a room with walls at 70 F, but I assure you, it would not be comfortable at all. Rather, though the energy deposited by those X-rays may keep you warm, your body would rapidly suffer irreversible damage as it absorbs such quantities of ionizing radiation, breaking up molecular bonds, destroying your cells’ DNA. What is quantum? Which things fit the definition of quantum? There are things that are “quantized”, which is to say, exhibit behavior that comes in distinct chunks, and the branch of physics that deals with these things is called therefore “quantum physics”. But to the extent that it even touches on the concept of “quantum”, it’s a consequence, not a foundation. Not anymore. At first, quantum physics was mostly empirical. Yes, it was based on the idea that atoms emit or absorb energy in such discrete chunks, or quanta. This was observed. This led, for instance, to Planck’s famous radiation law, which marks the dawn of quantum physics. But over time, we became a tad more sophisticated. Less then thirty years after Planck initiated his revolution, the “new” quantum theory of Heisenberg and Schrödinger emerged. It was no longer about atoms emitting and absorbing quanta, but something far more fundamental: the mathematical representation of the state of a physical system. In classical physics, constituent parts of a physical system can be characterized by a) where they are, b) how they move. In other words, their positions and their speed (or momenta). These can be represented by numbers. A position is just a set of coordinates. A velocity is a vector that can be characterized by a set of coordinates. As I said, numbers. Then comes the “new” quantum mechanics, which represents positions and momenta by… well, something else. Matrices in Heisenberg’s case, function operators in Schrödinger’s, but the bottom line is the same: These things are not numbers. Specifically, they do not behave like numbers do under multiplication. Take the momenta p and positions q of a system. In classical physics, we can multiply these numbers together and get a result that does not depend on the order of multiplication: p q = q p , or p q − q p = 0. But this is not how positions and momenta behave in the new quantum physics. They obey instead the relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and, well, i = √ − 1 . This leads to all sorts of weird consequences, which have been confirmed experimentally. Among other things… well, quanta. Take one of the simplest physical systems, a simple oscillator (the so-called harmonic oscillator). Describe it in terms of these non-commuting variables and you get a weird result: The oscillator cannot have arbitrary energies. Its energy is discretized, going up or down by one unit, or quantum at a time. Electrons in an atom are well described by such oscillators as a mathematical model. So there we have it, the quantized behavior of how atoms emit or absorb energy. But quantum physics in general is not really about quanta. It’s not about chopping things up into small units. That might have been the original inspiration more than a century ago, but it has become something much more nuanced. Planck’s quanta are still there, but as a consequence, not as a building block, of the theory. There are plenty of “quantum” systems that have no quantized behavior. E.g., a free particle can have any energy; nothing “quantized” there. The fundamental statement of the theory is not about quanta; it is about the behavior of those key variables, the positions and momenta of a physical system, and how this behavior is described by the mathematics of noncommuting things, as opposed to the mathematics of simple numbers. Like it or not, that is how Nature behaves, as demonstrated by countless experiments. That said, when we go beyond simple quantum mechanics into the realm of quantum field theory, things change a bit. A field, like the electromagnetic field, can be described as a sum of, well, pure waves really, by way of what is called a Fourier-transform. Each of these pure waves behaves like a harmonic oscillator, which we know how to describe using quantum physics. Each of these harmonic oscillators is characterized by those distinct chunks of energy by which the oscillator’s energy can increase or decrease. In quantum field theory, these distinct chunks of energy (and possibly other conserved properties, like charge or angular momentum) turn out to be none other than the things we’ve know, we’ve observed, as particles! So there you have it: elementary particles come closest to the concept of “quantum”. (Indeed, sometimes we even say so explicitly: e.g., “photons are the quanta of the electromagnetic field.”) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If motion is non-absolute, why are we looking for dark energy when energy isn't required for a 'perceptually'-expanding universe? Don’t be misled by a name. “Dark energy” is neither “dark” nor “energy”. Blame physicists for coming up with inappropriate names and sticking with them long after they exhausted their usefulness. (The inappropriate names, not the physicists.) It’s called “dark” when in fact it should be called “invisible”. Or “completely transparent, not interacting with known forms of matter or light”. But… okay, “dark”. As to “energy”, well, insofar as general relativity is concerned, at least in the context of cosmology, everything is “energy”: that is, everything is characterized by its energy-content and pressure. Which is to say, everything in a non-empty universe is assumed to be well approximated by the concept of an “isotropic perfect fluid”. So “dark energy” is really a “completely transparent, non-interacting medium with negative pressure, characterized by the equation of state p = − ρ , “ which is to say, its pressure is the negative of its energy density. Contrast this with “dark matter”, which is a “completely transparent, non-interacting medium with no pressure.” Sometimes also called “dust”. Motion has nothing to do with it. The equations of cosmology match observations (in particular, minute fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background and the large-scale statistical distribution of matter) if the universe is roughly 70% “dark energy” and 30% “dust” (which also includes ordinary matter, by the way, since its pressure is negligible compared to relativistic mediums.) As to the expansion, nothing perceptual about it. Things are flying apart. Not something abstract like “the universe”, or “space” or the “cosmos”. Literally, things: galaxies, clusters of galaxies are flying apart, which is to say, the average distance between them increases over time, their density decreasing over time. If an airliner (e.g. Boeing 747 800) was magically transported to the same altitude as the International Space Station, how quickly would it depressurise? It would be surprisingly slow. Keep in mind that at normal cruising attitude, outside pressure is already pretty low, less than 20% of sea level pressure. So the pressure-induced stress on the aircraft fuselage at ~400 km altitude (where the ISS orbits) would not be much greater than during cruise. So nothing dramatic happens… other than, of course, all engines failing due to lack of air, along with any auxiliary power units (APUs), so the only things operating on that aircraft at this time would be minimum emergency equipment running off battery power. Having said that, assuming that the aircraft is properly pressurized and there are no undue leaks or valves left open, the leakage rate of a well-maintained aircraft seems to be surprisingly low. I found some data: According to a conversation at PPRuNe Forums, it took some 30 minutes to reach a cabin pressure altitude of 10,000 ft in one new aircraft. In the same conversation, someone else quotes 500 ft/min as the leakage rate of a brand new A320. So even a conservative guesstimate suggests at least 15 minutes before pressure drops within that fuselage to dangerously low levels. Which creates an interesting scenario. If that aircraft was magically lifted to 400 km altitude without being accelerated to orbital speed, it won’t stay up that high for very long. Rather, it’d start to fall, and fall rather rapidly since there is no noticeable air resistance. In fact, without air resistance it would reach the ground in something like 5 minutes. Of course in reality, it would run into denser and denser air that would ultimately slow its descent. The question is, would it be survivable? No, it’s not about heat shields. Heat shields are needed for spacecraft re-entry because they enter the atmosphere at orbital speed. This hypothetical aircraft of ours would start off slow, and never reach speeds at which heating due air resistance becomes a major concern. Even so, it probably (almost certainly?) would not survive, especially considering that at this point, the pilots have no control over the aircraft; there is no power, and of course no air for the control surfaces to operate on. Before the pilots can do anything useful, the airplane would have to descend to an altitude where there is enough oxygen to start up at least an APU. That would be, what, maybe 20 km or less? Far too late. Much earlier, the aircraft would be falling at supersonic speeds, at an uncontrolled attitude, encountering denser and denser layers of air. (Recall that the space shuttle Columbia broke up at an altitude of ~60 km; it was much faster of course, but it should tell you that even at 60 km, there’s already more than enough air to cause structural failure for a fast-falling aircraft.) However, if by some miracle, that aircraft makes it to 20–25 km altitude without losing important bits like a wing or two, and an APU could be restarted, I think it is conceivable that the pilots might be able to regain control and slow the aircraft down without substantially more structural damage, as it continues to descend. I have no idea (I don’t think anyone does) how a 747 would fly at Mach 3 at 20–25 km but who knows, perhaps it would manage to stay attached to most of its wings as the pilots bleed altitude and speed? (I am thinking of China Airlines Flight 006 as I am writing down these somewhat optimistic words.) The point is, should that miracle happen, during the 5–10 minute ordeal at no time would cabin pressure drop to a level that would seriously harm or kill the occupants, unless something else (structural failure, a stuck valve, etc.) causes the cabin to depressurize rapidly at an altitude that is still too high for the oxygen masks to be effective (above ~20 km outside pressure is low enough for our blood to boil at body temperature). The big if is whether or not the airplane would survive the fall through the upper atmosphere in one piece; and the answer is that it almost certainly would not. Is it possible to use telescopes to observe the event horizon and beyond of a black hole, or does the gravity of the black hole absorb all light before it reaches us? Here is the thing about black holes: No photon ever leaves the event horizon. This would be true even if we had pre-formed, “primordial” black holes in this universe, with fully formed event horizons. This is the very nature of an event horizon, nothing, not even light, can ever come from one. Add to this the fact that an actual, astrophysical black hole that forms as a result of gravitational collapse never really completes the process. Its event horizon remains forever in the future of any observer outside. So to “see” its event horizon, you’d need not a telescope but first and foremost, a time machine, to bring a signal from the future to the present! In short, no. Not even with an all-powerful telescope can you see what’s not actually there, namely light leaving a black hole’s event horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If it turned out that white holes don't exist, how would it affect physics? It would confirm something that we think we already know, namely that this universe is reasonable well-behaved and causal. You see, a white hole is a time-reversed black hole. Take the “time reversed” bit seriously. A white hole isn’t a white hole because it repels things. Its gravity is just as attractive as a black hole’s gravity. (A time-reversed orbit is still an orbit, not a hyperbolic escape trajectory.) The reason why things can’t fall into the white hole is because they are not in the white hole in the future. (This is the time reversed version of a similar statement about black holes: Things can’t come out of black holes because they are not in the black hole in the past.) So if a white hole were to exist, it would mean that your own life is determined by your future: You can’t make the decision to fly into a white hole because you are not in the white hole in the future. Sounds illogical? Well, in a sense it is, if we think causality is logical. But white holes don’t care about causality. Their presence literally implies that the future determines the past. So be grateful perhaps that there are no white holes (as far as we know) in this universe. That means that our universe can behave, well, in a manner we consider “logical”, which is to say, causality applies and no effects precede their causes. What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? Intelligence has nothing to do with it. “Classical” has a lot to do with it. Let me explain. A “classical” entity: a human, a cat, a brick, a video camera, has well-defined states. A brick is either on the table or on the floor, never both. A human is either moving or standing still, never both. A cat is either alive or dead, never both. (Putting aside pointless philosophical musings about cats being, after all, “quantum” since they consist of a very large but finite number of uncorrelated quantum degrees of freedom… true, but for all practical intents and purposes, bricks, cats, etc., are classical. Any quantum behavior is averaged out to the extent that it vanishes.) A “quantum” entity is different. A quantum entity does not have a classically defined position or momentum. Rather, it has a state. That state, which may be described (depending on your mathematical preference) by a vector in an abstract space, or by a fancy wavefunction, can be used to calculate the probability of finding that quantum entity with a certain value for its position or momentum when it interacts with something classical. Let me explain how. What the equations actually tell us is that the state of the quantum entity evolves such that it is constrained by its past, present, and future interactions, including interactions with classical things such as bricks, cats or humans. Quantum physics is manifestly nonlocal (this is the essence of Bell’s famous theorem) so it is subject to constraints that can be arbitrarily far in space or time, yet curiously, somewhat counterintuitively, it remains causal (it is not possible to arrange the future to induce an observable influence on the past). A quantum entity is neither a particle nor a wave, it just displays behaviors of both under the right circumstances. The state of that quantum entity obeys a wave equation including the ability to exhibit interference patterns. But when a quantum entity interacts with a classical thing, the interaction may be localized, creating the appearance of something resembling a miniature cannonball, i.e., a particle. Concerning the double-slit experiment, the quantum entity may be a photon or an electron (so let me just call it an electron from now on), which is confined by three things: a) the location and time of emission; b) the slits; and c) the location and time of detection. These are the constraints that determine the wavefunction that characterizes this electron’s state. One possible interpretation, obviously inspired by the uncomfortable consequence of quantum nonlocality, namely that the location and time of detection is one of the constraints characterizing the system, is to take that constraint out of the picture initially. We then describe the state of an electron that is characterized by the location and time of emission, and the presence of the slits. The resulting wavefunction can be used as a probability amplitude, characterizing the probabilities of possible locations and times for the electron’s detection. When we actually do detect the electron, the picture changes: We now have a new wavefunction that is also constrained by the location and time of detection. This rather abrupt replacement of one wavefunction with another we call “wavefunction collapse”. Now it is true that this interpretation requires an intelligent creature, such as a human who prefers this probabilistic interpretation (the Copenhagen interpretation). But apart from some (not generally accepted) extensions of the quantum theory that treat wavefunction collapse as a physical process, the collapse is only a clumsy mental aid. It is a philosophical musing, not physical reality. In reality, that electron was always governed by a wavefunction subject to nonlocal constraints (again I stress, this is the fundamental essence of Bell’s theorem.) So to sum up, a quantum entity (photon, electron, etc.) is neither a particle nor a wave; its state is governed by a wave equation so it sometimes exhibits the consequences of wave-like behavior; its interactions may be highly localized, giving the impression of a particle; and intelligent observers have nothing to do with this unless we buy into the controversial concept of objective collapse (of the wavefunction), and perhaps not even then. How do you know there is no speed of gravity? For the same reason I know there is no speed of water. I look at a glass of water, and it’s perfectly still. I look at a fast-flowing river, and the water is moving, well, very fast. I look the icy moon Europa of the planet Jupiter, and I see tremendous quantities of water ice moving very, very fast around Jupiter. Or maybe not moving at all if I happened to stand on Europa’s icy surface? So what exactly is the speed of water? On the other hand, I do know, for instance, the speed at which certain influences travel in water. Though it is affected by things such as temperature or salinity, sound travels roughly 1.5 kilometers a second in water. That is true in the glass of water I hold in my hands, it is true in the rivers and oceans, it is even true on Europa. So then, gravity. A static gravitational field has no speed. Why would it? Speed measures change. There is no change when the field is static. However, if you are wondering how fast changes in the gravitational field travel, far from any specific source of gravitation: Why, it’s the same speed at which changes in the electromagnetic field travel, far from any sources (electric charges). It’s called the vacuum speed of light, light being the word we associate with a particular range of frequencies of electromagnetic waves, which also include radio waves, infrared and ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays. Similarly, changes in the gravitational field travel in the form of waves, and far away from sources (masses), those waves are transverse waves traveling at the same vacuum speed of light. But that is not the “speed of gravity” any more than the speed of light is the “speed of electromagnetism”. Forgive the pedantry here, but it is important to convey the correct impression: namely that speed is associated with the rate at which changes travel, the static field itself has no speed associated with it.

What would it look like if gravitational waves came at us and were strong enough to be visible? Like if two ton618 sized black holes collided nearby. Just so that the wave could make a visible distortion in space. What would it look like? Visible is the wrong word to use here as there’s nothing to see. However, you might hear it! Let us assume a “clean” collision, two black holes with no other material, so no visible light, no gamma rays, nothing that would kill you or vaporize you, just gravitational waves. And you get close enough. Well, when the merger is between two stellar black holes, the peak gravitational wave emission happens at frequencies that fall well within the audible range. Which means that if you are close enough (but not too close!), you might actually hear (literally, hear) the result, as the passing time-varying tidal effect moves wiggles parts of your body, including all those little bits inside your ear. The technical nature of the waves (transversal waves traveling at the vacuum speed of light) is different from sound waves (longitudinal pressure waves in a medium, traveling much slower than the vacuum speed of light) but the effect is similar: mechanical excitation of bits that are particularly sensitive to the frequencies in question. Mind you, don’t get too close: Just as a powerful blast of sound waves can kill you, so can a too powerful gravitational wave. Now that’s two stellar black holes. You mentioned TON 618. They are much too big for anything audible to happen. The frequencies in question would be measured in a microhertz or less, which is to say, a period measured in days. You would neither hear nor see anything until you are close enough to experience powerful tides on a time scale of days. So if such an event were to occur in our relative stellar neighborhood, the effect could be an unexplained tide, which, depending on how close we are to the event, could be minor or devastating.
